title: The word brought home to Achadh àrsaidh
summary: The second of the two Achadh àrsaidh boats that met the strangers' ships off the north-west cape turns home and brings the word to its households, while Lachlann Odhar's boat leads the strangers' ships south toward Cuan shean. Achadh àrsaidh is the first place on the island to hear of the strangers, and it hears of them from its own fishers.

title: Lachlann Odhar leads the ships down the coast
summary: Lachlann Odhar steers south from the north-west cape the length of a winter day, past the empty headlands of the north-west, with the strangers' ships shortening sail to keep behind him. He runs his boat up the shingle at Cuan shean after dark and wakes the custodians.

title: The ships stand off Cuan shean in the westerly weather
summary: A run of westerly gales keeps Na Trì Longan standing off and on beyond the bar of Cuan shean for many days. The town watches them from the dunes, and the custodian Oighrig nic Leòid forbids any boat to put off to them or any fire to be lit on the strand.

title: Oighrig nic Leòid gives water on the shingle
summary: Edmund Harrow wades ashore at Cuan shean with an empty cask, and the custodian Oighrig nic Leòid gives him and his eleven men water from the town well under the old law of the shore. She has seven casks filled and refuses anything more on her own word.

title: The rider from Cuan shean reaches Cathair dhearg
summary: A rope-maker's son of Cuan shean rides the valley road to the capital in a day with Oighrig nic Leòid's letter on the ships. The clerk of the council reads it standing. The council's answer, two days later, bids Cuan shean feed the strangers, keep them apart and decide nothing.

title: Three of Harrow's men buried above the tide-line
summary: Three of the strangers, sick from the long voyage, die on the strand below the dunes at Cuan shean. Their own people bury them above the tide-line with a reading from a book and kneeling on the sand, while the town's children watch from the dunes.

title: Harrow's men mend nets on the dunes
summary: Recovered from their sickness, the strangers penned below the dunes at Cuan shean begin mending the fishers' nets spread on the strand, unasked. The fishers learn from them a flat knot that does not slip, and call it the strangers' knot.

title: Buttons traded for fish on the strand
summary: The first trade between the island and the strangers begins on the strand at Cuan shean, yellow-metal coat buttons for fish. The custodians forbid it twice and it goes on behind the dunes; at last Oighrig nic Leòid lets it be, and the fishwives wear the buttons on cords.

title: Manannan's priests keep the tide-prayer through the forty days
summary: Through the forty days the strangers are fed below the dunes, the priests of Manannan at Seann Skell say their prayer to keep the sea shut at every tide without missing one. The harbour scribe enters their number each week, nine, with the weather and the thinness of Ceò Mhanannain.

title: The strangers sheltered in the net-lofts
summary: With the autumn gales the custodians of Cuan shean let the strangers off the open strand into the net-lofts along the harbour. The ships lie in the harbour with their yards sent down and a few hands aboard. The roll enters the lofts as a shelter for the winter and no leave.

title: Oighrig nic Leòid falls ill
summary: At Samhain the custodian of Cuan shean takes a cough that goes into her chest, and by an Dùbhlachd she cannot leave her bed. Custodians riding up to the council at Cathair dhearg stop at her bedside on the way.

title: Oighrig nic Leòid's letter to the council from her sickbed
summary: From her bed at Cuan shean Oighrig nic Leòid writes to the council that she gave the strangers water under the law of the shore and nothing more on her own word, and that a leave given in the roll cannot be ungiven. She asks that it be read before the vote. The clerk notes it received.

title: The leave read on the strand at Cuan shean
summary: A custodian of Cuan shean reads the council's leave to the strangers from an upturned boat on the strand, with a stranger who has learned some words in the net-lofts putting it into his own tongue. The strangers cheer three times and begin to send their ships' yards back up.

title: The struck line in the council roll
summary: Bidden to strike from the council's roll the old sailors' saying about the quarter of the sea, the clerk at Cathair dhearg strikes it and writes beneath the striking what he was told to strike, so that the next clerk should know. The saying stands in the roll so, struck and unanswered.

title: Lachlann Odhar's words at the harbour wall
summary: Going home at last to Achadh àrsaidh in an Gearran, Lachlann Odhar stands on the harbour wall at Cuan shean and says aloud that the ships came out of the quarter Cabhlach an Scaraidh sailed into. Nobody on the harbour answers him, and he puts out for the north.
